# How the length cap drives memory, and how little it drives time

A 36-epoch training run consumed all application memory and took a machine down. This walks the sequence-length cap up one rung at a time to find out what actually caused it, with a ceiling that kills the rung rather than the machine.

The answer is the length cap, and the useful part is how differently it drives the two things people conflate: memory and time.

## How it was measured

- **Corpus** — German bitext, 100,000 training pairs, SentencePiece, longest pair 266 subwords (p50 23)
- **Model** — batch 64, `d_model` 256, 3 layers, 8 heads
- **Runtime** — MPS (Apple Metal, unified memory), 64 GiB machine, bucketing on, AMP off
- **Each rung** — 2 epochs, seed 1, its own process

`device held` is what the allocator holds, not what the model needs: on Metal that reserve is taken from the machine's own RAM, so it is the figure that decides whether anything else can run. `reclaimed` is what `empty_cache()` returns.

## The ladder

| cap | device held | reclaimed | peak RSS | s/epoch | batches | pairs truncated |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 ¹ | 0.31 GiB | 0.25 | 0.91 | 136.2 | 1,562 | 99.04% |
| 10 | 1.28 GiB | 1.23 | 1.02 | 138.1 | 1,562 | 89.38% |
| 20 | 1.43 GiB | 1.38 | 0.97 | 147.3 | 1,561 | 56.82% |
| 40 | 2.52 GiB | 2.46 | 1.36 | 167.8 | 1,560 | 16.91% |
| 80 | 6.46 GiB | 6.40 | 2.11 | 183.0 | 1,559 | 2.70% |
| 100 | 9.60 GiB | 9.54 | 2.27 | 192.0 | 1,560 | 1.30% |
| none | 35.80 GiB | 35.73 | 3.54 | 192.0 | 1,559 | 0.00% |

¹ Not quotable as evidence about scaling: see the caveat below.

## What the cap at 100 actually buys

This is the result the ladder was built to get, and it is a better bargain than it looks.

| | cap 100 | no cap |
|---|---|---|
| device held | **9.60 GiB** | 35.80 GiB |
| seconds/epoch | 192.0 | 192.0 |
| pairs truncated | 1.30% | 0% |

**73% of the memory cost removed for 1.30% of the data**, at identical wall clock.

The reason is that peak memory is set by the *longest* batch, not the median one. Pairs above 100 subwords are a 1.30% sliver of the corpus, but while they are present every epoch must allocate for them. Clipping the tail is therefore cheap in data and large in memory, which is precisely the trade a length cap exists to make.

It also explains why wall clock does not move: the same number of batches still runs, and only the few longest ones get shorter.

## Two levers, different shapes

Across the quotable range — cap 10 to no cap (effective 266 subwords) — **memory moves 28x while time moves 1.39x.**

So they are separate levers, and the one sentence worth giving a student is:

> **Batch count sets how long an epoch takes. The length cap sets whether it fits at all.**

If a session dies, the first thing to look at is the length cap, not the epoch count and not the batch size.

## Growth is not quadratic in the cap

Attention is quadratic in sequence length, so the cap was expected to be too. It is not, because attention is only part of the footprint: embedding and feed-forward activations are *linear* in length and dominate until sequences grow long enough for the quadratic term to overtake them.

| interval | length factor | memory factor | implied exponent |
|---|---|---|---|
| 10 → 20 | 2.00x | 1.12x | 0.16 |
| 20 → 40 | 2.00x | 1.76x | 0.82 |
| 40 → 80 | 2.00x | 2.56x | 1.36 |
| 80 → 100 | 1.25x | 1.49x | 1.78 |
| 100 → none | 2.66x | 3.73x | 1.35 |

## Caveats, which are the most reusable part of this

- **These are MPS unified-memory figures.** On Metal the allocator's reserve is taken from the machine's own RAM, so it is not comparable to CUDA device memory as an absolute number. Treat the *shape* as transferable and the magnitudes as machine-specific. Confirming the shape on the accelerator students are actually given is Task #118.
- **Two epochs per rung.** Enough for memory and seconds per epoch, which stabilise immediately. Not enough to say anything about convergence, so this does not settle Task #110's question about whether validation loss is still falling at 36 epochs.
- **`device held` is a reserve, not a requirement.** It reflects peak allocation plus whatever the pool kept, so it overstates what the model strictly needs. It is the right number for 'will this run beside anything else', and the wrong one for 'how big a model could I fit'.
- **Validation loss rises with the cap** across these rungs, which is not a regression. A tighter cap truncates more of every sentence, leaving an easier and less meaningful prediction task. Loss is not comparable across rungs, and only the within-rung trend means anything.

## Corrections

- **The first attempt measured nothing.** Rungs nominally at 5 and 10 tokens agreed to three decimal places on memory, time and loss, because `create_dataloaders` was discarding the `Config` it was handed and both ran at the default cap. Fixed in torchlingo PR #84; the rungs were rerun.
- **The crash was attributed to unreleased cache, then to length, and length is right.** With the cap honoured, a 5-token run holds 0.31 GiB where the same command uncapped holds 35.80. Task #108 (nothing calls `empty_cache`) is real but secondary: it returns the spike after it has been taken, which on unified memory is usually too late.
- **The 512 positional ceiling never bound anything** on this corpus, whose longest pair is far shorter. The run labelled uncapped is the longest-pair measurement, not a 512-token one.
- **Growth was predicted as quadratic in the cap and is not.** The exponent table above shows it climbing toward the quadratic only at the long end.

## Open question this does not answer

Whether this fits a paid Colab session, which is the question Assignment 8 actually turns on. That needs Colab's ceiling measured on the accelerator students are assigned (Task #118) and cannot be answered from this machine. Until both halves exist, no memory claim belongs in the A8 handout — only the ordering of the levers, which is solid.
